overview.description: Anrufen (meaning 'to call') is an elegant Austrian trick-taking game belonging to the Marriage family. It is distinguished by its 'Call-a-Card' partner selection and a simplified scoring system where only 'Gwisse' (Aces, Tens, and the Last Trick) carry numerical value. It combines the secret partnerships of bridge with the point-collecting mechanics of MariÃ¡Å¡.

history.origins: A descendant of the 18th-century French game 'Mariage', which spread across the Austro-Hungarian Empire. The Austrian version settled into a 24-card format common in the Salzburg and Alpine regions.
timeline: 1700s: Mariage becomes a court favorite in Europe.
1850s: Austrian regional versions (Anrufen, KÃ¶nigrufen) diverge from the Czech MariÃ¡Å¡.
1930s: Documented as a staple of Alpine tavern play.
history.evolution: The game simplified the complex point-counting of 32-card games to prioritize 'Marriages' and the pivotal 'Last Trick'.
history.cultural: Commonly played for small stakes or tokens in Austrian 'GasthÃ¤usern'. The 'Call' is often made with great ceremony to reveal the secret partner.

setup.deck: 24 cards. Using French suits (A-10-K-Q-J-9) or German suits (A-10-K-O-U-9).
setup.equipment: Standard 32-card deck (remove 7s and 8s), score sheet or tokens.
setup.dealing: Each player is dealt 6 cards in batches of 3-3. Bidding rotates clockwise starting from the dealer's left.

rules.objective: As a member of the bidding side, capture 'Gwisse' points and declare 'Marriages' to reach the target of 50 points (or more for higher bids).
rules.gameplay: 1. **Bidding**: Players bid in levels: Simple (50+), 100 Points, All Tricks, or No Tricks. 2. **Calling**: The high bidder names a card (e.g., 'Ace of Hearts'). The holder is their partner. The suit of that card is TRUMP. 3. **The Play**: Bidder leads the first trick. Players MUST follow suit. If void, they MUST trump. If possible, they must head the trick (win it). 4. **Marriages**: A player holding the King and Queen (or Over) of a suit can declare a 'Marriage' when leading the first card of that hand. 40 points for trump marriage, 20 for others. 5. **Last Trick**: Worth 10 bonus points.
keyRules: Follow-Suit & Must-Trump: Strict trick-taking rules apply.
Secret Partner: The partner's identity is revealed only when they play the called card.
The Winner: First card led by the bidder initiates the trump suit based on the call.
Gwisse: Aces and Tens are the only valued cards (10 pts each).

strategy.basic: If you hold many trumps but lack the Ace, call your own Ace's suit to ensure your partner has a powerful entry card.
strategy.intermediate: Last Trick Management: Save your highest trump (usually the Ace) for the final trick, as capturing it is worth the same value as an entire Ace or Ten.
strategy.advanced: Defensive Marriage Spoiling: If you suspect an opponent has a Marriage, lead that suit early to force them to play one of the marriage cards defensively before they can declare it.
tips: Always count the 'Gwisse'. There are only 8 counting cards in the deck; knowing who has taken three of them is key.
In 'Simple' games, your priority is the 50-point threshold. Don't take unnecessary risks for extra tricks.

difficulty.easy: Doesn't understand 'Must-Trump' rules. Fails to declare marriages.
difficulty.medium: Bids aggressively with two Aces. Understands 'Last Trick' importance.
difficulty.hard: Remembers all 24 cards played. Predicts the partner's strength based on the 'Accept' or 'Contra' during bidding. Strategically leads 'Nine' of trumps to extract opponents' Tens.

considerations: AI must support 'Secret Partner' logicâ€”it might be playing against its own partner for several tricks.

trumpConfig.overtakingRule: Players must follow suit if possible. A player who cannot follow suit must play a trump if able, and must beat the highest card so far played to the trick when possible. The trick is won by the highest trump in it, or if it contains no trump by the highest card of the suit led.

trickConfig.leadRestrictions: Bid winner leads the first trick; afterward, the winner of each trick leads the next.

customActions.description: Deal 6 cards in batches to each player.
Call Ace-King to determine trump and partner.
Announce marriage (K-Q of trump) when playing.

engine.deckDescription: One standard 24-card deck: six ranks (ace, ten, king, queen, jack, nine) in each of four suits. French or German suit names may be used; no jokers. Used for this calling (Anrufen) variant of Schafkopf or similar games.
engine.suitDescription: Four suits (typically French: spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs; or German: acorns, leaves, hearts, bells). Each suit has six cards; trump and plain-suit order depend on the bid and the called suit.
engine.rankDescription: Six ranks per suit: ace, ten, king, queen, jack, nine. In trump the order often differs (e.g. jack and nine high); the called ace determines the partner in Anrufen. Standard 24-card ranking applies within each mode.

hero.title: ANRUFEN
hero.subtitle: The Alpine Marriage
hero.tagline: A game of secret partners, 'Gwisse' points, and high-altitude strategy.

synthesis.shortDescription: Master the art of 'Calling' in this Austrian classic. Coordinate with a secret partner, declare marriages for 40 points, and capture the 'Gwisse' to dominate the table.

prompts.human: Welcome to Anrufen. You have 6 cards. Check for marriages (King + Queen)! Will you bid a simple game or go for 100 points? Remember, your first lead sets the trumps and names your partner. Make sure to capture the Aces, Tens, and the last trick!
prompts.ai: Game: Anrufen. Type: Secret Partnership (Marriage Group). Players: 4. Rules: 24 cards (A-10-K-Q-J-9). Must follow, trump, and beat. Points: Aces/Tens=10, Last Trick=10. Marriages: 40/20. Goal: 50+ points.

scoring.description: Total points are 90 (8 Aces/Tens + Last Trick) plus any marriage bonuses.
scoring.winCondition: The bidding side wins if they reach 50 points in a Simple game, or their specific high-bid target.

penalties.Bid Failed: The bidding side loses the wager/tokens to the opponents.

scoring.splitRules: If 'Simple' bid totals 45-45, the bidder loses (needs 50 to win).

nullReasons.cardValues: Anrufen scores only Aces, Tens, and a 10-point last trick; per-card values are explained in scoring.description rather than a rank map.
